From Atomic to Composite: Reinforcement Learning Enables Generalization in Complementary Reasoning

Sitao Cheng, Xunjian Yin, Ruiwen Zhou, Yuxuan Li, Xinyi Wang, Liangming Pan, William Yang Wang, Victor Zhong

Paper ↗Code ↗

In a controlled reasoning setting, RL helps models combine internal knowledge with new context when supervised training has first established both component skills.

01 / The research question

A high score can hide the missing skill

Suppose a document identifies the new editor of a magazine, while the editor’s business partner and that partner’s occupation are facts stored in a model. Answering the full question requires crossing between context and memory. Success on either source alone leaves this transition untested. Ordinary question-answering benchmarks make the diagnosis difficult: a model might already know the complete answer from pretraining.

The study therefore builds synthetic biographies and separates which relations are learned through parameters from which arrive in context. Questions follow paths of two to five relations. This makes the location of each required fact explicit, so a failure to combine sources can be distinguished from the absence of the underlying information.

03 / Inside the method

Control what is new at test time

The evaluation separates three kinds of novelty. IID questions use a practiced relational path with different entities. Composition questions recombine relations that appeared in other training paths. Structural zero-shot questions contain a relation absent from the training questions, although its facts remain available in biographies or context. This final category tests a broader transfer than changing the names in a familiar template.

The key intervention is the preparation before RL. One model receives SFT on parametric and contextual reasoning separately; another learns complete complementary questions. Both then receive the same composite RL examples, with GRPO rewarded only for the final answer. A further comparison matches SFT sample counts and hop distributions, reducing the possibility that an easier dataset or more reasoning steps explains the advantage.

The interactive example follows the paper’s editor-and-business-partner question. Switching between parametric, contextual, and combined tasks makes the required source of each fact explicit. A separate comparison shows measured SFT accuracy across the three generalization splits; the worked answer is not presented as a new model result.

  1. 01

    Separate the skills

    Synthetic biographies distinguish facts learned in model parameters from facts supplied in context.

  2. 02

    Train, then combine

    Teach both atomic skills with SFT, then reward correct answers on questions requiring their combination.

  3. 03

    Test new relations

    Evaluate familiar paths, new combinations, and relations absent from training questions.

04 / Reading the evidence

The prerequisite matters beyond the starting score

  • 90.30% → 18.41%

    Composite SFT: IID to zero-shot

    Direct composite supervision performs well on familiar paths but drops sharply on the structural zero-shot split.

  • Atomic skills first

    Condition for RL generalization

    RL generalizes better after learning both component skills than after direct composite supervision in the tested setting.

In Section 5.2, models with comparable initial complementary-task scores respond differently to the same 12,800 RL examples. Learning both atomic skills provides a stronger foundation than limited direct composite supervision. Starting from the atomic model, further SFT, LoRA, and RL all help, but SFT is strongest on familiar paths while RL is strongest on the structural zero-shot split.

The pass@k analysis adds a separate test: after atomic preparation, the RL advantage persists even with 512 samples. After composite preparation, the curves approach each other. This is evidence of different changes to the answer distribution, but finite sampling cannot prove that a solution had exactly zero probability beforehand. The practical result is the curriculum effect; identifying the internal mechanism remains open.

Research summary

Reinforcement Learning (RL) following Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) has become the standard paradigm for post-training Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the mechanism by which RL contributes to reasoning capabilities—whether it incentivizes the synthesis of new skills or merely amplifies existing behaviors—remains a subject of intense debate. In this work, we investigate this question through the lens of Complementary Reasoning, a complex task that requires integrating internal parametric knowledge with external contextual information. Using a controlled synthetic dataset of human biographies, we strictly decouple this ability into two atomic skills: Parametric Reasoning (relying on internal knowledge encoded in model parameters) and Contextual Reasoning (depending on novel information provided in the context window). To rigorously assess capability boundaries, we evaluate generalization across three distinct levels of difficulty: I.I.D., Composition, and Zero-shot settings. We find that while SFT is sufficient for in-distribution performance, it struggles with out-of-distribution generalization, particularly in Zero-shot settings where relational combinations are novel. Crucially, we identify the SFT Generalization Paradox: Models supervised solely on the composite task achieve near-perfect in-distribution accuracy (90%) but collapse on out-of-distribution generalization (18%), indicating their reliance on rote memorization of path shortcuts. In contrast, we find that RL acts as a reasoning synthesizer rather than a probability amplifier. However, we uncover a strict atomic prerequisite: RL can only synthesize these complex strategies if the base model has first mastered the independent atomic skills (Parametric and Contextual) via SFT. These findings challenge the view of RL as a mere amplifier, suggesting that given sufficient atomic foundations, RL can actively synthesize complex reasoning strategies from learned primitives without explicit supervision on such complex strategies. This indicates that decoupled atomic training followed by RL offers a scalable path to generalization for complex reasoning tasks. Code and data will be at https://github.com/sitaocheng/from_atomic_to_composite.
